query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post-fabrication high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) treatment applied to additively manufactured refractory HEA components will improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by reducing residual stresses and defects introduced during selective laser melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy components fabricated by selective laser melting, characterized by fabrication-induced defects, residual stresses, and slight compositional inhomogeneities.
generation.intervention: Application of an HPHT post-processing treatment.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied immediately after SLM fabrication under controlled HPHT parameters (optimized high pressure and temperature conditions) designed to promote microstructural refinement without inducing unwanted phase transformations. This treatment is intended for HEA components used in high-temperature aerospace and energy applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces and reduced porosity.
generation.mechanism: The HPHT treatment promotes plastic deformation, residual stress relief, and enhanced diffusion that together densify the material and reduce fabrication-induced defects (such as pores and microcracks), thereby improving both dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated SLM HEA components, those receiving HPHT post-treatment will exhibit enhanced dimensional precision (i.e., reduced warping and distortion) and improved mechanical integrity (i.e., higher strength and ductility, with lower defect density).
generation.baseline: As-fabricated HEA components produced via selective laser melting without any post-processing show measurable deviations in dimensions, residual stresses, and micro-defects limiting their mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory HEAs produced by SLM under conditions typical to aerospace and energy applications; the optimal HPHT parameters may vary with specific alloy compositions and device geometries.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise HPHT conditions (pressure level, temperature, and duration) required to achieve the desired microstructural improvements without triggering adverse phase changes, as well as how scalable these conditions are for different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured refractory HEA samples via selective laser melting. Subject one set to the proposed HPHT post-processing treatment while retaining the other as untreated controls. Ensure homogeneous processing conditions (except for the HPHT intervention) across all samples.
measurements: Dimensional measurements using high-resolution 3D scanning to quantify deviations and distortions.
Microstructural characterization via scanning electron microscopy and X-ray computed tomography to assess defect density (porosity and microcracks).
Mechanical testing (tensile strength and ductility) to quantify improvements in mechanical integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPHT-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision (i.e., reduced geometric deviations), lower defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the untreated controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
